name: Jonah
bio:
Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath Hepher, was a prophet of the LORD. During the reign of Jeroboam (son of Jehoash), king of Israel, Jonah had prophesied that the LORD would restore Israel's border from Lebo Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah; the LORD fulfilled this through Jeroboam, out of compassion for Israel's bitter affliction rather than willingness to blot out Israel's name (2 Kings 14:25-27). His own remarkable story — called to preach to Nineveh, fleeing by sea, swallowed by a great fish, and wrestling with God's mercy toward a foreign city — is told in detail in the book that bears his name.

## 📖 Core Story: Fleeing to Tarshish

When the LORD told Jonah to go preach against Nineveh's wickedness, he fled instead by ship toward Tarshish, in the opposite direction. The LORD sent a violent storm; when the terrified sailors cast lots and discovered Jonah was the cause, he told them to throw him overboard, admitting he was running from the LORD. They reluctantly did, the sea instantly calmed, and the awestruck sailors offered sacrifices to the LORD. A great fish then swallowed Jonah, who spent three days and nights in its belly praying in desperate repentance and thanksgiving, until the LORD had the fish vomit him onto dry land (Jonah 1:1-2:10).

## 📖 Core Story: Nineveh's Repentance and Jonah's Anger

Commanded a second time, Jonah went to Nineveh and proclaimed that the city would be destroyed in forty days. To his evident surprise, the entire city — from its king down to its animals — repented in sackcloth and fasting, and God relented from destroying it. Furious rather than pleased, Jonah complained that he had fled precisely because he knew God would show mercy to this foreign enemy, and asked to die. When God made a plant grow to shade him and then let it wither, Jonah grieved its loss more than he cared about Nineveh's hundreds of thousands of people; God used the plant to rebuke Jonah's narrow, self-centered compassion and affirm his own mercy toward even a great pagan city (Jonah 3:1-4:11).
